claim: Gap junctions are widely distributed in the brains across species.
source: Gap junctions are widely distributed in the brains across species and play essential roles in neural information processing.
evidence: This is a general statement about gap junctions that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Gap junctions play essential roles in neural information processing.
source: Gap junctions are widely distributed in the brains across species and play essential roles in neural information processing.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by established scientific consensus.

claim: Gap junctions are present in Drosophila Kenyon cells (KCs).
source: Using a flight simulator paradigm and genetic tools, we found that gap junctions are present in Drosophila Kenyon cells (KCs), the major neurons of the mushroom bodies (MBs), and showed that they play an important role in visual learning and memory.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from dye coupling and genetic manipulation experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Gap junctions in Kenyon cells play an important role in visual learning and memory.
source: Using a flight simulator paradigm and genetic tools, we found that gap junctions are present in Drosophila Kenyon cells (KCs), the major neurons of the mushroom bodies (MBs), and showed that they play an important role in visual learning and memory.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from visual learning and memory experiments with genetic manipulations.

claim: A single pair of MB output neurons (MBONs) possess a gap junction connection to KCs.
source: Furthermore, we identified a single pair of MB output neurons (MBONs) that possess a gap junction connection to KCs, and provide strong evidence that this connection is also required for visual learning and memory.
evidence: This claim is supported by dye coupling and electrophysiological recording data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The gap junction connection between MBONs and KCs is required for visual learning and memory.
source: Furthermore, we identified a single pair of MB output neurons (MBONs) that possess a gap junction connection to KCs, and provide strong evidence that this connection is also required for visual learning and memory.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral experiments showing impaired visual learning and memory when innexins are knocked down in β'2mp neurons.

claim: A gap junction consists of an intercellular channel that is formed by two hemichannels, each containing six homo- or heteromeric protein subunits.
source: A gap junction consists of an intercellular channel that is formed by two hemichannels, each containing six homo- or heteromeric protein subunits.
evidence: This is a statement of established structural knowledge about gap junctions.

claim: Gap junction protein subunits belong to the connexin or pannexin gene families in vertebrates and the innexin (inx) gene family in invertebrates.
source: These subunits belong to the connexin or pannexin gene families in vertebrates and the innexin (inx) gene family in invertebrates.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the molecular composition of gap junctions across species.

claim: Gap junctions allow the circulation of small molecules, such as ions and cAMP.
source: Gap junctions allow the circulation of small molecules, such as ions and cAMP (Hervé and Derangeon, 2013; Phelan and Starich, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The function of gap junctions in noise reduction is critical for visual and olfactory processing in mammals.
source: The function of gap junctions in noise reduction (DeVries et al., 2002; Veruki and Hartveit, 2002) and neuronal synchronization (Bloomfield and Völgyi, 2009; Pereda et al., 2013) is critical for visual and olfactory processing in mammals.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The function of gap junctions in neuronal synchronization is critical for visual and olfactory processing in mammals.

claim: The synchronization of neurons through the function of gap junctions was proposed to play a key role in cognitive processes, such as perception, attention, as well as learning and memory.

claim: There are 8 types of inx genes expressed in Drosophila.

claim: Mushroom bodies (MBs) are a pair of clearly distinguishable structures in the Drosophila brain.
source: Mushroom bodies (MBs) are a pair of clearly distinguishable structures in the Drosophila brain, and play critical roles in cognition, such as olfactory coding (Lei et al., 2013; Masse et al., 2009), olfactory learning and memory (Davis, 2011; Wolf et al., 1998),context generalization (Liu et al., 1999), feature extraction (Peng et al., 2007), reversal learning (Ren et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2012), and value based decision making (Tang and Guo, 2001; Zhang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila neuroanatomy.

claim: Kenyon cells (KCs) are the major neurons of MBs.
source: Kenyon cells (KCs), the major neurons of MBs, are the main components of the MB neural network, which is composed of dopamine neurons (DAs), MB output neurons (MBONs), and other cells (Aso et al., 2014a, b; Tanaka et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge about mushroom body anatomy.

claim: Kenyon cells are the main components of the MB neural network, which is composed of dopamine neurons (DAs), MB output neurons (MBONs), and other cells.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Visual learning and memory was impaired when α/β neurons of KCs, driven by 17d-GAL4, were hyperpolarized.
source: We found that visual learning and memory was impaired when α/β neurons of KCs, driven by 17d-GAL4, were hyperpolarized, and the memory was restored when GAL4 activity was blocked in MBs by MB247-GAL80 (Figure 1B, upper panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Memory was restored when GAL4 activity was blocked in MBs by MB247-GAL80.
source: We found that visual learning and memory was impaired when α/β neurons of KCs, driven by 17d-GAL4, were hyperpolarized, and the memory was restored when GAL4 activity was blocked in MBs by MB247-GAL80 (Figure 1B, upper panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Hyperpolarizing α'/β' neurons with MB370B-GAL4 abolished visual learning and memory.
source: Hyperpolarizing α'/β' neurons with MB370B-GAL4, γ neurons with MB131B-GAL4, or α/β and γ neurons of KCs with MB247-GAL4 also abolished visual learning and memory (Figure 1B lower panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Hyperpolarizing γ neurons with MB131B-GAL4 abolished visual learning and memory.
source: Hyperpolarizing α'/β' neurons with MB370B-GAL4, γ neurons with MB131B-GAL4, or α/β and γ neurons of KCs with MB247-GAL4 also abolished visual learning and memory (Figure 1B lower panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Hyperpolarizing α/β and γ neurons of KCs with MB247-GAL4 abolished visual learning and memory.
source: Hyperpolarizing α'/β' neurons with MB370B-GAL4, γ neurons with MB131B-GAL4, or α/β and γ neurons of KCs with MB247-GAL4 also abolished visual learning and memory (Figure 1B lower panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: When synaptic release was impaired via expression of shibirets1 in KCs by 17d-GAL4, visual learning and memory was intact.
source: However, when synaptic release was impaired via expression of shibirets1 (shits1) (Kasuya et al., 2009; Praefcke and McMahon, 2004; van der Bliek and Meyerowitz, 1991) in KCs by 17d-GAL4, MB370B-GAL4 or MB247-GAL4, visual learning and memory was intact (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: When synaptic release was impaired via expression of shibirets1 in KCs by MB370B-GAL4, visual learning and memory was intact.

evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: When TNT was expressed in α/β neurons (17d-GAL4), fly's visual learning and memory remained intact.
source: When TNT was expressed in α/β neurons (17d-GAL4) or all KCs (VT61721-GAL4), fly's visual learning and memory remained intact (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: When TNT was expressed in all KCs (VT61721-GAL4), fly's visual learning and memory remained intact.
source: When TNT was expressed in α/β neurons (17d-GAL4) or all KCs (VT61721-GAL4), fly's visual learning and memory remained intact (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Visual learning and memory were abolished when Kir2.1 was expressed in KCs using MB247–GeneSwitch GAL4 driver.
source: As shown in Figure 1D, visual learning and memory were again abolished.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Visual learning and memory remained intact in flies of which MBs were ablated by hydroxyurea.
source: However, in agreement with previous report (Wolf et al., 1998), visual learning and memory remained intact in flies of which MBs were ablated by hydroxyurea (HU) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and a citation to previous research.

claim: Visual learning and memory might be influenced in real time by non-chemical-synaptic transmission in MBs.
source: Taking together, these results indicated that visual learning and memory might be influenced in real time by non-chemical-synaptic transmission in MBs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results showing that hyperpolarization impairs memory but blocking chemical synapses does not.

claim: Electrical-synaptic transmission via gap junctions was a plausible candidate for the observed effects on visual learning and memory.
source: We therefore speculated that electrical-synaptic transmission via gap junctions was a plausible candidate for such observation.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the experimental observations.

claim: Knockdown of inx6 in 17d-GAL4-labeled neurons resulted in impairment of fly learning and memory.
source: As shown in Figure 2A, knockdown of inx6 in 17d-GAL4-labeled neurons resulted in impairment of fly learning and memory.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Flies with the knockdown of inx4, inx5 or inx6 were not able to achieve performance indices significantly different to zero.
source: Flies with the knockdown of inx4, inx5 or inx6 were not able to achieve performance indices significantly different to zero, whereas the control groups did.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The effect of gene downregulation was eliminated when the RNAi expression were blocked by MBGAL80.
source: The effect of gene downregulation was eliminated when the RNAi expression were blocked by MBGAL80.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Visual learning and memory was impaired in flies with the knockdown of inx4, inx5 or inx6 in MB247-GAL4-labeled KCs.
source: Visual learning and memory was also impaired in flies with the knockdown of inx4, inx5 or inx6 in MB247-GAL4-labeled KCs (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: When inx4 was knocked down in adults, visual learning and memory was not affected.
source: When inx4 was knocked down in adults, visual learning and memory was not affected, whereas adult knockdown of inx5 or inx6 exerted significant effects (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Adult knockdown of inx5 exerted significant effects on visual learning and memory.
source: When inx4 was knocked down in adults, visual learning and memory was not affected, whereas adult knockdown of inx5 or inx6 exerted significant effects (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Adult knockdown of inx6 exerted significant effects on visual learning and memory.
source: When inx4 was knocked down in adults, visual learning and memory was not affected, whereas adult knockdown of inx5 or inx6 exerted significant effects (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: INX5 and INX6 are post-developmentally required in the α/β lobes of MBs for visual learning and memory.
source: Therefore, INX5 and INX6 are post-developmentally required in the α/β lobes of MBs for visual learning and memory whereas INX4 may contribute to MB development instead, thus affecting visual learning in an indirect manner.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results showing differential effects of adult vs. developmental knockdown.

claim: INX4 may contribute to MB development, thus affecting visual learning in an indirect manner.
source: Therefore, INX5 and INX6 are post-developmentally required in the α/β lobes of MBs for visual learning and memory whereas INX4 may contribute to MB development instead, thus affecting visual learning in an indirect manner.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observation that inx4 knockdown affects learning only when done developmentally.

claim: Knockdown of inx5 or inx6 in MB370B split-GAL4-labeled α'/β' neurons impaired visual learning and memory.
source: As shown in Figure 2E, knockdown of inx5 or inx6 in α'/β' neurons abolished visual learning and memory, and knockdown of inx genes in γ neurons had no effect (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Knockdown of inx genes in γ neurons had no effect on visual learning and memory.
source: As shown in Figure 2E, knockdown of inx5 or inx6 in α'/β' neurons abolished visual learning and memory, and knockdown of inx genes in γ neurons had no effect (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The gap junctions composed of INX5/6 in α/β and α'/β' neurons are involved in visual learning and memory in Drosophila.
source: Together, these results suggest that the gap junctions composed of INX5/6 in α/β and α'/β' neurons are involved in visual learning and memory in Drosophila.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results showing that knockdown of inx5/6 in these neurons impairs visual learning and memory.

claim: Dye coupling was observed in 14 out of 143 successfully stained brains.
source: Among the 143 successfully stained brains, 64 α/β neurons, 40 α'/β' neurons and 39 γ neurons were loaded with dye. Dye-coupled neurons were observed in 14 brains (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from dye coupling experiments.

claim: In 10 out of the 14 brains with dye coupling, dye coupling was observed between the same subtype of KCs.
source: In 10 out of the 14 brains, dye coupling was observed between the same subtype of KCs, including 8 α/β-α/β, 1 α'/β'-α'/β' and 1 γ-γ (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from dye coupling experiments.

claim: In 4 of the 14 brains with dye coupling, dye coupling was observed between different KC subtypes.
source: In 4 of the 14 brains, dye coupling was observed between different KC subtypes (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from dye coupling experiments.

claim: Gap junctions exist in both the calyx and the lobes that link KCs of the same or different subtypes as well as some non-KC neurons.
source: Together, these results suggest that gap junctions exist in both the calyx and the lobes that link KCs of the same or different subtypes as well as some non-KC neurons.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the dye coupling experimental results.

claim: Dye coupling was observed in 5 brains of the wild type flies but in none of the inx5/6 knockdown flies.
source: Dye coupling was observed in 5 brains of the wild type flies but in none of the inx5/6 knockdown flies (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from blind dye coupling experiments shown in Table 1.

claim: The probability of failing to observe any coupling in the knockdown group by chance is about 0.00065.
source: Assuming a binomial process with p=5/38 (k = 5; n = 38 in the control group) to observe false-positive dye coupling, the probability of failing to observe any coupling in the knockdown group (k = 0; n = 52) is about 0.00065, suggesting a small likelihood for false-positive labeling.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the dye coupling data.

claim: Upon hyperpolarization in KCs, a hyperpolarization was measured in MBON-β'2mp neurons labelled by MB002B-GAL4 or MB011B-GAL4.
source: Upon hyperpolarization in KCs, we measured a hyperpolarization in MBON-β'2mp neurons labelled by MB002B-GAL4 or MB011B-GAL4.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recording data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The hyperpolarization response in MBON-β'2mp neurons remained unchanged after the application of tetrodotoxin (TTX).
source: This response remained unchanged after the application of tetrodotoxin (TTX), which blocks chemical synapses by suppressing action potentials (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recording data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Laser-induced hyperpolarization disappeared when gap junctions were blocked by 2-octanol (2-OCT).
source: In contrast, laser-induced hyperpolarization disappeared when gap junctions were blocked by 2-octanol (2-OCT) (Bohrmann and Haas-Assenbaum, 1993), and was recovered after 2-OCT was washed out (Figure 4C), while 2-OCT application could induce slight hyperpolarization (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recording data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Laser-induced hyperpolarization was recovered after 2-OCT was washed out.
source: In contrast, laser-induced hyperpolarization disappeared when gap junctions were blocked by 2-octanol (2-OCT) (Bohrmann and Haas-Assenbaum, 1993), and was recovered after 2-OCT was washed out (Figure 4C), while 2-OCT application could induce slight hyperpolarization (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recording data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: β'2mp MBONs are able to receive inputs from KCs through electrical synapses.
source: These results suggest that β'2mp MBONs are able to receive inputs from KCs through electrical synapses.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the electrophysiological recording results showing TTX-insensitive, 2-OCT-sensitive hyperpolarization.

claim: In 3 of the 35 recorded brains, dye coupling was observed between a β'2mp neuron and an α'/β' neuron.
source: In 3 of the 35 recorded brains, dye coupling was observed between a β'2mp neuron and an α'/β' neuron.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from dye coupling experiments during whole-cell recording.

claim: Visual learning and memory were ablated following inx6 knockdown in β'2mp neurons using two set of RNAi strains from independent sources.
source: As shown in Figure 6, visual learning and memory were ablated following inx6 knockdown using two set of RNAi strains from independent sources.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Downregulation of inx5 with the RNAi strain TRiP. JF02877 abolished visual learning and memory.
source: Downregulation of inx5 with the RNAi strain TRiP. JF02877 also abolished visual learning and memory (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: A gap junction network containing KCs and β'2mp neurons is crucially involved in visual learning and memory.
source: Taken together, our results provide strong evidence that a gap junction network containing KCs and β'2mp neurons is crucially involved in visual learning and memory.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined results of dye coupling, electrophysiology, and behavioral experiments.

claim: Gap junctions in KCs may contribute to noise reduction, especially those that connect KCs of the same subtype with common inputs.
source: Similar to their function as a low-pass filter in reducing noise during sensory processing (DeVries et al., 2002; Veruki and Hartveit, 2002; Zhang et al., 2013), gap junctions in KCs may contribute to noise reduction, especially those that connect KCs of the same subtype with common inputs.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on analogy to known functions of gap junctions in other systems.

claim: Gap junctions that connect KCs of different subtypes may serve as a communication channel that links multiple processing units.
source: Considering that the different KC subtypes have diverse functions (Guven-Ozkan and Davis, 2014; Vogt et al., 2014; Yi et al., 2013), gap junctions that connect KCs of different subtypes may serve as a communication channel that links multiple processing units.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the observation of inter-subtype gap junctions and citations to previous research on KC subtype functions.

claim: The gating, assembly, internalization and degradation of gap junction channels can be delicately modulated by phosphorylation.
source: The gating, assembly, internalization and degradation of gap junction channels can be delicately modulated by phosphorylation (Laird, 2005; Moreno, 2005; Solan and Lampe, 2005); and these regulation may underlie memory encoding in MB-MBON networks.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The regulation of gap junction channels may underlie memory encoding in MB-MBON networks.
source: The gating, assembly, internalization and degradation of gap junction channels can be delicately modulated by phosphorylation (Laird, 2005; Moreno, 2005; Solan and Lampe, 2005); and these regulation may underlie memory encoding in MB-MBON networks.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the potential mechanism of memory encoding.

claim: Approximately 10% of all KCs possess active gap junction connections.
source: Our results showed that approximately 10% of all KCs possess active gap junction connections, which is very likely to be an underestimate of their density, due to the following reasons: 1) The dye coupling efficiency may be restricted with the gating of gap junction channels, which might not be always open and which might be delicately modulated; 2) filling an entire neuron with sufficient amounts of dye is a difficult and time-consuming (1–2 hr) procedure, due to the slender morphology of their neurites.
evidence: This is an inference based on the dye coupling experimental results.

evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the rates of dye coupling and electrical coupling observed in the experiments.
